beats.spoken: Next to the number on your sunscreen, the EU wants a word: one of four categories.

The European Commission has recommended this since 2006. Sunscreen efficacy should be shown in a simple, clear and meaningful way. So every number should belong to a category: low, medium, high or very high. Each category should match a standardised level of protection against UVB and UVA.
The table is clear. SPF 6 and 10 count as low. 15, 20 and 25 as medium. 30 and 50 as high. And 50 plus as very high.

The numbers are deliberately limited. Instead of lots of values, only a few should appear on labels, so products are easier to compare. A measured value between 30 and 49.9, for example, is labelled as 30. From a measured value of 60, it's labelled 50 plus.
And here's the key point: the category should be at least as visible as the number. It's not meant to be small print.

rows.text: category at least as visible as the number

beats.spoken: For you, that means: don't just read the number, read the word next to it. It tells you at a glance which protection level the product is in.
Read the category first, then apply. Beauty knowledge, clearly explained: follow Dewlane.
